lessons.title: What is JavaScript? Your first program

content.explanation: JavaScript is the language of the web. It runs in every browser and, with Node.js, on servers too. Programming means giving the computer precise step-by-step instructions. console.log() prints a value so you can see what your program is doing.

exercises.prompt: Print your name and your city on separate lines.
Print a sentence that contains double quotes.
exercises.hint: Wrap it in single quotes or use backticks.

interview_questions.a: In browsers (via a JS engine like V8) and on servers with Node.js.

interview_questions.q: Is JavaScript the same as Java?
interview_questions.a: No. They are different languages with different designs.

content.real_world: console.log is the first debugging tool every web developer uses, in browser DevTools and in Node.

content.explanation: Variables store values. Use const for values that will not be reassigned and let for values that will change. Avoid var in new code. Names use camelCase, like studentName.

examples.title: const and let
const cannot be reassigned
examples.code:
const x = 1;
// x = 2;  // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

exercises.prompt: Store your age in a variable and log a sentence with it.
Swap two variables using a temporary variable.

common_mistakes: Using a variable before declaring it.
Using = when you mean === in comparisons.

interview_questions.q: Difference between let, const and var?
interview_questions.a: let and const are block-scoped. const cannot be reassigned. var is function-scoped and hoisted, so it is best avoided.

interview_questions.q: Does const make an object immutable?
interview_questions.a: No. The binding cannot change, but the object's contents can.

content.real_world: Shopping cart totals, logged-in user info and UI state are all variables.

content.explanation: Primitive types: number, string, boolean, undefined, null (plus bigint and symbol). Use typeof to inspect a value. Operators: + - * / % **. Always compare with === (strict equality). Convert text to a number with Number().

examples.title: typeof
examples.code: console.log(typeof 5, typeof "5", typeof true, typeof undefined);

exercises.prompt: Convert the string "42" to a number and add 8.
Convert 250 minutes into hours and minutes.

common_mistakes: Adding a string and a number: "5" + 3 gives "53".
Assuming typeof null is 'null' (it is 'object', a historic quirk).

interview_questions.a: === does not coerce types, so results are predictable.

interview_questions.q: What is the difference between null and undefined?
interview_questions.a: undefined means no value was assigned. null is an intentional empty value.

content.real_world: Form inputs arrive as strings, so converting types correctly is a daily task in web development.

content.explanation: Conditions let the program choose a path. JavaScript runs the first block whose condition is truthy. Combine conditions with && (and), || (or), ! (not). Falsy values: false, 0, empty string, null, undefined, NaN.

examples.title: Grade
Combine
examples.code:
const age = 20, hasId = true;
if (age >= 18 && hasId) console.log("Allowed");

exercises.prompt: Print whether a number is positive, negative or zero.
Check if a year is a leap year.
exercises.hint: Divisible by 4, except centuries unless divisible by 400.

common_mistakes: Using = instead of === in the condition.
Forgetting the brackets around the condition.
Forgetting that an empty string or 0 is falsy.

interview_questions.a: Any value that is not falsy, for example non-empty strings and non-zero numbers.
condition ? a : b, a short if/else that returns a value.

content.real_world: Login checks, feature flags, discounts and form validation all depend on conditions.
